verdict.rationale: On the narrow initiation question the cited Greek consistently puts the divine act before the human movement toward God. John 6:44 and 6:65 join the negated potential verb dynatai to the condition ean me, so coming is impossible unless the Father first draws (helkyse, aorist subjunctive) or has given (dedomenon, perfect passive). Rom 9:16 negates ou tou thelontos, the one willing, with the adversative alla relocating the ground to tou eleontos theou, and Phil 2:13 names God as energon even to thelein, the willing itself. John 15:16 reverses the order, ouch hymeis exelexasthe all ego exelexamen, and 1 John 4:19 marks God protos, first. Acts 16:14 has the Lord dienoixen the heart so as to prosechein, the opening preceding the attending. These priority markers foreclose the semi-Pelagian claim that the human takes the unaided first step. The distinct and narrower cooperation question, whether the prior work fully effects the willing or enables a will that still freely consents, is not ranked by the vocabulary, hence medium confidence.

scripture.force: The negated potential verb dynatai joined to the condition ean me makes coming impossible apart from a prior act of the Father. That act is helkyse, the aorist active subjunctive of helkyo, draw or drag. Across its eight canon occurrences helkyo names a forceful effectual drawing, dragging Paul and Silas to the marketplace in Acts 16:19, dragging from the temple in Acts 21:30, drawing a sword in John 18:10, hauling the net in John 21:6 and 21:11, so the verb here describes an initiating divine pull, not a mere offer, and the coming follows it rather than precedes it.

The same negated dynatai plus ean me construction grounds the ability to come in the perfect passive participle dedomenon, it has been given, ek tou patros, from the Father. This verse uses didomi rather than helkyo, and the perfect tense marks a settled prior gift as the standing precondition of the human approach, again placing the divine act first.

The clause negates ou tou thelontos, the one willing, and oude tou trechontos, the one running, then with the strong adversative alla locates the determining ground in tou eleontos theou, the God who shows mercy. Human willing, the very faculty the semi-Pelagian first step would exercise, is expressly displaced as the operative cause and the merciful God is named instead.

The causal gar grounds the preceding exhortation in God who is energon, the present active participle of energeo, working in believers both to thelein, the willing, and to energein, the working, for his eudokia, good pleasure. Including the infinitive to thelein within God's operation places the gracious work prior to and beneath the act of the will itself, which is the precise point the proposition asserts.

The verse reverses the order of initiative directly, ouch hymeis me exelexasthe, you did not choose me, all ego exelexamen hymas, but I chose you. Both verbs are eklegomai in the aorist middle, and the negation of the human subject paired with the emphatic ego makes the divine choosing the prior and operative act, with the human relation following from it rather than originating it.

The clause hemeis agapomen, we love, is grounded in hoti autos protos egapesen hemas, because he first loved us. The adverbial protos, first, makes God's love explicitly prior in order to the human love, so the human response is presented as derivative of and consequent upon a divine act that precedes it.

The narrative states that ho kyrios dienoixen ten kardian, the Lord opened the heart, of Lydia, with the infinitive prosechein, to attend, expressing the result. The verb dianoigo occurs nine times in the canon and consistently names a supernatural opening done to a recipient, opening eyes, Scriptures, minds and ears in Luke 24:31, 24:32, 24:45 and Mark 7:34. The divine opening precedes and produces the attending, so the human attention is consequent on the prior divine act.

Salvation is by grace through faith, and the demonstrative touto is qualified as ouk ex hymon, not from yourselves, but theou doron, the gift of God. The framing sets the gift over against human origination, consistent with grace preceding the human response rather than assisting an autonomous first move.

The phrase ouk ex ergon excludes works as the source, and the hina clause states the purpose that no one may boast, kauchesetai. Removing all ground of boasting in the human contribution reinforces that the initiative does not originate in the human will, though this verse addresses the source of salvation broadly rather than the will-grace ordering specifically.

complicating_texts.resolution: The cross reference for John 6:44 uses the same verb helkyo, kago ean hypsotho ek tes ges pantas helkyso pros emauton, I will draw all to myself. Some read pantas, all, as universalizing the drawing so that it no longer functions as a discriminating prior cause. That reading bears on the extent of the drawing, not on its priority. Lexically helkyo still names a divine act that precedes coming, so the proposition about grace initiating the movement is sustained regardless of how the scope of pantas is resolved.

The cross reference grounds Romans 9:16 in election me ek ergon, not from works, before the twins had done anything good or bad. This strengthens rather than complicates the priority reading, since it removes prior human action as the basis. The lexical force of ou tou thelontos in 9:16 is consistent with it.

The immediately preceding verse commands katergazesthe, work out your own salvation, which on a cooperative reading keeps a real human acting alongside the divine working of 2:13. This does not complicate the priority claim, since the gar of 2:13 grounds the human working in God who first energei the willing. The human activity is presented as flowing from the prior divine operation, not as an unaided first step, so the ordering the proposition asserts holds while leaving the cooperation question open.

variants.note: None of the cited verses fall within the ingested ECM window of 3 John, so no apparatus units were examined here. The marked readings on the bundle surface forms, for example the bracketed me in John 6:44 and the patros note in John 6:65, touch the surrounding words but not the lexemes dynatai, helkyse, dedomenon, energon, thelontos, exelexamen, protos or dienoixen that carry the verdict, so the reading is treated as variant robust.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the priority markers as decisive against the semi-Pelagian first step. The negated dynatai plus ean me in John 6:44 and 6:65, ou tou thelontos in Romans 9:16, energon to thelein in Philippians 2:13, the reversed eklegomai in John 15:16, the protos of 1 John 4:19 and the dienoixen that produces prosechein in Acts 16:14 all locate the initiating act in God. On this lens the human cannot supply the first movement toward God by natural ability, because every cited construction places a divine act prior to and as the enabling ground of that movement.

Grants the same priority that the texts assert, since helkyo, didomi, energeo, eklegomai and dianoigo each name a real prior divine initiative, so this lens also denies the bare semi-Pelagian first step. It then distinguishes a narrower question the vocabulary does not settle, whether the prior grace fully effects the willing or enables a will that still freely and non-coercively consents. On this reading prevenient grace goes first and is necessary, yet a genuine human assent remains within the response, so the priority is affirmed while the completeness of the prior work is held open.

hermeneutics.notes: Both lenses agree that the cited lexemes place a divine act before the human coming and therefore both reject the semi-Pelagian unaided first step. They diverge only on the narrower and distinct question of whether that prior work fully effects the willing or enables a will that still consents. The shared lexical floor, which is what this proposition asserts, is that grace initiates the movement. The contested point lies beyond the proposition, in the completeness of that prior work, which the words do not rank.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine whether the sinner can take the first step toward God by natural ability with grace then assisting, or whether a prior gracious work of God must enable any movement of the will toward Him.
stem_audit.notes: The stem encodes its own conclusion in the clause rather, the prior gracious work of God enables any movement of the will toward Him, which loads the answer before the evidence is weighed. The verdict was derived on the neutralized form, which poses the ordering as an open question. On the lexical merits the priority markers place the initiating act in God, which forecloses the specific semi-Pelagian first step. The narrower cooperation question, whether the prior work fully effects the willing, is not ranked by the vocabulary, which is reflected in medium confidence and the competing lens block.

lay_summary: The Greek of these verses keeps putting God's action before the person's first move toward him. In John 6:44 and 6:65 the words say no one is able, dynatai, to come unless, ean me, the Father first draws, helkyo, or has given, a perfect form marking a settled earlier gift. The same verb for draw is used elsewhere for hauling a net and dragging people to court, so it is a real pull, not just an offer. John 15:16 flips the order plainly, you did not choose me but I chose you. First John 4:19 says we love because he first, protos, loved us. In Acts 16:14 the Lord opened, dianoigo, Lydia's heart so that she paid attention, the opening coming before the attending. Romans 9:16 says it does not depend on the one who wills but on God who shows mercy, and Philippians 2:13 says God is the one working in believers even the willing itself. Taken together these priority words say the first step is God's, which is exactly the point in question, because semi-Pelagianism is the claim that the person makes the first move by natural ability and grace only helps afterward. The words push against that. There is still a narrower and separate question the vocabulary does not settle. Once grace has gone first, does that prior work by itself fully produce the willing, or does it enable a will that then genuinely and freely consents. Careful readers divide here, and both sides agree the divine act comes first. They differ only on how complete that prior work is. Because the verbs clearly make the initiating act God's, the evidence affirms that grace must begin the movement, while the completeness of that prior work stays open, so confidence is medium rather than high.
